after.title: Preprint: Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
after.authors: Dragostinov, Y.; Hsu, R. E.; Ennis, G. W.; Londono-Correa, D.; Schwaba, T.; Nivard, M. G.; Tucker-Drob, E. M.
after.abstract: Polygenic indices (PGIs) are downwardly biased in their predictive accuracies in independent samples due to the presence of estimation error in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) from which they are constructed. By performing GWAS of the same phenotype in independent samples, we obtain to error-corrected estimates of PGI prediction accuracy, which we use to estimate the extent to which different PGI construction methods (unadjusted, Clumping, LDpred2-inf, LDpred2-auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) index total single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) heritability. To ensure practicality of this approach when individual-level data from the original GWAS are not available, we provide a means of synthetically splitting existing GWAS summary statistics into independent halves. In both simulated and empirical data, we find that advanced PGI construction methods that produce enhanced uncorrected prediction accuracies (often by shrinking individual SNP effects towards zero or exactly to zero) also produce deflated error-corrected prediction accuracies. LDpred2-inf, which most closely resembles a multiple regression estimator to account for linkage disequilibrium without further aggressive shrinkage, consistently produces PGIs with relatively lower uncorrected prediction accuracies but higher error-corrected prediction accuracies that nearly fully recover SNP heritability. We show that PGI construction methods that implement aggressive shrinkage may also provide biased patterns of associations with collateral phenotypes, irrespective of error correction. By providing a means of straightforwardly obtaining error-corrected estimates of prediction accuracy using PGIs derived from standard GWAS summary statistics, we have highlighted an uncommonly recognized bias-variance tradeoff associated with the choice of PGI construction methods.

after.authors: Perez-Elena, M. A.; Salvoro, C.; Matias, D.; Satari, L.; Puiggros, M.; Zugasti, D.; Alonso-Parrilla, L.; Torrents, D.
after.abstract: X chromosome (Xchr) contribution to complex traits remains incomplete, due to its unique inheritance pattern and its inactivation mechanism. Therefore, we gathered data from 800,000 individuals from the UK Biobank and dbGaP, and performed a sex-stratified phenome-wide association study of Xchr variation across 3,741 complex traits. Heritability analyses revealed sex-specific patterns and an overall involvement of Xchr in complex phenotypes. We identified 6,531 loci significantly associated with 402 complex traits, with a higher proportion of associations consistent with dominant inheritance than observed for autosomes. Although effect directions were largely concordant between sexes, loci with significant effect-size differences were enriched for escape-gene associations. Escape genes were depleted among trait-associated loci and strongly enriched for risky disease effects. These association patterns enabled prediction of escape status for unannotated genes. This overview of Xchr contribution to complex traits suggests inactivation escape as a clear risky feature for females.

after.authors: Zhao, T.; Wu, G.; Hoffman, M. M.; Belzil, V. V.
after.abstract: Background. We examined transcriptomic (gene expression-based) aging in postmortem central nervous system (CNS) tissues from donors across the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-frontotemporal dementia (FTD) spectrum and investigated the molecular and cellular features underlying disease-associated differences in transcriptional aging clocks. Methods. Six transcriptomic clocks (RNAAgeCalc DESeq2, GTExAge, Pearson and GenAge; Pasta REG and age-shift) were applied to 2,235 RNA-sequencing samples from 609 donors across 11 CNS regions, with adjustment for age and tissue-specific technical variables. We compared transcriptional age across ALS, ALS-FTD, FTD, and controls, examining regional variation, gene-level contributions, cell composition, disease duration, and C9orf72 status, with independent validation of gene contributions in a cervical spinal cord cohort. Results. Disease-associated differences in transcriptional age varied by diagnosis, tissue, and clock. ALS and ALS-FTD showed the strongest differences in spinal cord, while FTD differences localized primarily to the frontal and temporal cortex. In ALS spinal cord, RNAAgeCalc DESeq2 estimates were lower than controls, whereas other clocks estimated higher transcriptional age when significant. CHIT1 was identified as the primary contributor to the DESeq2 transcriptional age decrease in ALS. Cell composition adjustment attenuated ALS spinal cord differences, reflecting microglial, lymphocyte, oligodendrocyte, and astrocyte signatures, though the lumbar GenAge increase in transcriptional age and DESeq2 decrease remained significant. The higher transcriptional age in ALS motor cortex also remained significantafter adjustment. Clinical associations were likewise clock dependent. Higher spinal DESeq2 age acceleration (AA) was associated with longer ALS duration, though this association was strongly influenced by the CHIT1 term. Higher GTExAge AA in cervical spinal cord, thoracic spinal cord, and occipital cortex was associated with shorter disease duration; no significant associations were observed for the other clock-tissue combinations or for ALS-FTD. No clock differed by C9orf72 repeat expansion status. Conclusions. In this study we found disease-associated differences in transcriptional age that localize to clinically relevant tissues. Differences in transcriptional aging across the ALS-FTD spectrum reflect interactions among clock architecture, disease-associated gene expression, tissue region, and cellular composition. Resolving these components reveals the biological context underlying divergent clock estimates and provides a framework for interpreting changes in transcriptional aging.

after.authors: Akter, S.; Guess, T.; Sarker, S.; Hockett, S. A.; Kiselica, A.; Hall, J.; Rao, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, United States
after.abstract: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), frailty, and fall risk often co-occur in older adults and share motor signs, yet they are screened and modeled separately. A unified model that predicts all 3 conditions from 1 sensor-based assessment could support earlier and more efficient screening, but such a model has rarely been developed or rigorously compared with separate models. Objective: This study aimed to develop a unified machine learning model that predicts MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from sensor-based motor-function data, compare it with separate single-label models, explain its predictions, and test its robustness. Methods: Community-dwelling older adults (n=79) completed a multimodal motor-function assessment with the Mizzou Point-of-Care Assessment System (MPASS), covering gait, sit-to-stand, static balance, step-down, and reaction time, with some tasks repeated under a dual-task condition. With demographic and family-history data, this yielded 59 features. Unified classifier-chain and single-label models were built with 5 algorithms across 6 modeling stages, evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation, and compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and paired bootstrap tests. The final model was explained with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and its robustness and the sufficiency of the sample size were tested with chain-input, chain-order sensitivity, domain-ablation, learning-curve, and power analyses. Results: With class weighting, the unified model had a higher mean AUC than the single-label models in 17 of 20 configurations and was never significantly worse, and it performed at least as well under nested model selection (0.615 vs 0.605; P=.58). The final extra trees model achieved a mean AUC of 0.645 (95% CI 0.569-0.722); discrimination was best for MCI (AUC 0.779, 95% CI 0.680-0.872) and lower for frailty (0.606) and fall risk (0.551). The model overestimated risk for all 3 outcomes, most for frailty. Most features (43/59, 73%), led by stride length, were shared across the 3 conditions, with consistent SHAP rankings in training and test participants ({rho}=0.99). Predicted frailty was the most important input for fall risk, and the 45 sensor features alone performed as well as the full model. Learning curves suggested that fall-risk prediction would benefit from more participants. Conclusions: A unified model predicted MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from one sensor-based assessment and performed as well as 3 separate models. It identified motor features shared across the conditions and used the link between frailty and fall risk. It performed best for MCI; with improvement for frailty and fall risk, recalibration, and external validation, such a model could support efficient screening of older adults for several conditions at once. KEYWORDS mild cognitive impairment; frailty; fall risk; machine learning; multi-label classification; classifier chain; gait; dual task; explainable artificial intelligence; Shapley additive explanations.

after.title: Preprint: Germline Variant Profiling of NA12878 Chromosome 22 Identifies the Loss-of-Function CYP2D6*3 and *4 Pharmacogenetic Alleles
after.authors: Mallick, S.; Singh, B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Biotecnika Info Labs Pvt Ltd., Bangalore, India
after.abstract: The approach used in this project to call germline variants from short-read sequencing data forms the basis of a great deal of current human genetics, whether it be in population studies or in diagnostic testing. A full germline variant-calling workflow according to the GATK Best Practices was constructed and carried out using public whole-genome sequencing data from the reference sample NA12878. In order to comply with the limitations of a laptop (an Intel Core i3, 8 GB of RAM, Ubuntu via WSL2), the analysis was limited to chromosome 22. The reads for chromosome 22 were streamed directly from the 1000 Genomes high-coverage CRAM file (run ERR3239334), converted into paired FASTQ files, checked using FastQC and MultiQC, and then cleaned with fastp. The cleaned reads were aligned to a GRCh38 reference containing only chromosome 22 using BWA-MEM, after which they were sorted, duplicates were marked and the base quality scores were recalibrated before variants were called with GATK HaplotypeCaller. The GATK-recommended hard filters were applied separately to SNPs and indels, and the variants that passed these filters were annotated using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) and summarised with a Python script. From the 81,599 raw calls, 73,570 (90.2%) survived the filtering process, and the transition/transversion ratio for the SNPs that passed filtering was 2.04. Of the annotated variant alleles, 98.9% were already present in the catalogue, 734 affected the coding sequence in 270 genes, and no variant corresponded to a pathogenic entry in ClinVar. Examination using IGV verified the read support for the selected high-impact calls, including the variants that define the CYP2D6*3 and *4 alleles, consistent with the published genotype of NA12878. The main limitations were a reduced effective depth of 8.6x, resulting from an incomplete read-collation step which retained about 31% of the read pairs, and the use of a chromosome-only reference.

after.title: Preprint: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data
after.authors: Gutierrez-Alvarez, I.; Rojas, A.; Calzadilla-Bertot, L.; Dopazo, J.; Romero-Gomez, M.; Loucera, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, Barcelona, Spain
after.abstract: Background. Short-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. Methods. From a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings. 771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores' high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. Its shape functions separated cancer-specific signal (AFP rising from 2 to 20 g/L, platelets below 150 x10^9/L) from liver failure (bilirubin above 51 mol/L, albumin below 35 g/L); a binary model showed only the first. Interpretation. An interpretable three-class model on routine data outperformed established scores for short-term HCC risk in cirrhosis, while showing whether each abnormal value points to cancer or to competing death.

after.title: Preprint: What Does an Agent-Run Clinic Cost? Protocol for a Prospective Observational Study of the Compute Cost of Completed Work in a Clinical Agent Fleet
after.authors: Elalfy, O.; Youssef, S.; Davids, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Wai Health Inc, Palo Alto, CA, United States; The London Wellness Clinic Ltd, London, United Kingdom
after.abstract: Background: Decisions about deploying large language model (LLM) agents in health care require the cost of completed work in production. Published evidence reports benchmark accuracy, benchmark-level cost, and time or financial outcomes for ambient documentation, and list prices alone do not determine the cost of completed work. To our knowledge, no deployed clinical agent fleet has published a measurement method that ties compute cost, latency, failures and retries to completed work. Objective: This study aims to estimate the compute cost of completed work by the orchestrated clinical agents of a deployed LLM agent fleet over a 12-week window of production telemetry, using estimators, data-quality gates and an analysis plan fixed before any window data are extracted for the study. Methods: The setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures in an earlier version were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. Results: The measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. No window data had been extracted for this study at submission. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. Extraction will begin no earlier than December 15, 2026, and the results are expected to be submitted for publication in 2027. Conclusions: The compute cost of completed clinical agent work can be specified as estimators over the run-level telemetry this deployment records, provided paired recording rows are separated from retries, missing terminal states are bounded and rounding of recorded cost is reported. This protocol fixes those estimators, and the reporting consequence of each known instrumentation defect, before extraction. Trial Registration: None. The analysis plan will be registered on Open Science Framework Registries before any window data are extracted for this study.

after.title: Preprint: Monitoring SNAP and Food Insecurity After the One Big Beautiful Bill Act: Early Evidence from a National Longitudinal Cohort
after.authors: Robertson, M.; Sanborn, J.; Penrose, K.; Nunez, J.; Arabadjis, S.; Silva, E.; Rane, M.; Parcesepe, A.; Nash, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: City University of New York Institute for Implementation Science in Population Health
after.abstract: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed in July 2025, restricted eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and expanded its work requirement, while federal tracking of food insecurity was scaled back. Using a national, community-based longitudinal cohort, we examined changes in SNAP receipt and food insecurity between August 2025 and March 2026 among 844 adults with household income below 200% of the federal poverty guideline, comparing participants in states that had and had not begun enforcing the expanded work requirement. SNAP receipt fell from 40.4% to 38.4%, and the share screening positive for food insecurity rose from 48.1% to 51.2%, with no detectable difference by state implementation timing. Adults who discontinued SNAP were as likely to be food insecure (71.1% in March 2026) and as worried about affording food, housing, and utilities as those who continued SNAP, and few had moved above 200% of the poverty guideline. These early findings suggest that need persisted after SNAP ended. As enforcement expands, policy makers should consider measures that keep benefits flowing to eligible people, such as extended certification periods and simplified recertification, and should support longitudinal monitoring of food insecurity.

after.authors: Yakubu, K.; Mukumbang, F.; Campain, A.; Cunich, M.; Atkins, E.; Coombes, J.; Hunter, K.; Bennett-Brook, K.; Madden, T.; McDonnell, M.; Thiraviarajah, A.; Lin, J.; Tan, I.; Forell, S.; Schierhout, G.; Jan, S.; Schneider, C. H.; Fotheringham, P.; Goodger, B.; Miller, E.; Haynes, L.; Woolfenden, S.; Eastwood, J.; Liu, H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The George Institute for Global Health, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia
after.abstract: Objectives: To describe a multi-methods explanatory evaluation protocol for Healthy Homes and Neighbourhoods (HHAN), an integrated care initiative for families experiencing health and social disadvantage in a Sydney health district. The evaluation will examine how and in what contexts HHAN influences health and social outcomes and will assess its value for money. Design: Multi-methods explanatory evaluation using linked administrative data, realist-informed interviews, yarning, and economic evaluation. Setting: A Sydney health district, including place-based hubs and partner sites involved in HHAN delivery or support. Participants: For the quantitative analyses, study participants will include participants of the HHAN program, linked family members in the Human Services Dataset, and a constructed counterfactual population. For the qualitative interviews and yarning, study participants will include service providers, program managers, policymakers, clients and carers involved in the HHAN program, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander participants where culturally appropriate and approved. Methods and analysis: Impact on health and social outcomes will be examined using linked administrative data with matching, weighting and regression-based approaches. A critical realist analysis of interview and yarning transcripts will explore program mechanisms of change and implementation conditions. Economic evaluation will estimate return on investment and cost-effectiveness where data permit. Findings will be integrated to explain patterns of impact and implementation across contexts. Ethics and dissemination: Ethics approval has been granted by the Aboriginal Health and Medical Research Council of NSW HREC (2137/23), Sydney Local Health District HREC (X23-0452 and 2023/ETH02445), and the NSW Population and Health Services Research Ethics Committee for data linkage, including waiver of consent for linked administrative data (2024/ETH01094). Findings will be shared through peer-reviewed publications, policy and service briefings, partner forums, community-facing outputs and Aboriginal governance channels. Trial registration number: Not applicable; this is an evaluation protocol and not a clinical trial. Author Approval: All authors have read and approved this protocol Competing Interests: We declare no competing interests Data Availability Statement: Not applicable as this is a study protocol Keywords: Health equity; integrated care; multi-methods; implementation; economic evaluation; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health.

after.title: Preprint: The effectiveness of the 'RecoverEsupport' digital health intervention in enhancing recovery from colorectal cancer surgery: RCT outcomes from the hospital admission.
after.authors: Wyse, R.; Viana da Silva, P.; Palazzi-Parsons, A.; Sansalone, E.; Forbes, E.; Robinson, S.; Johnston, S.-A.; Fakes, K.; Nolan, E.; Leigh, L.; Charlton, J.; Smith, S.
after.abstract: Background Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) guidelines improve recovery outcomes following colorectal (CR) cancer surgery. However, adherence to patient-led ERAS behaviours within the guidelines remains variable. Digital health interventions (DHIs) may increase adherence to these behaviours during the perioperative period. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a behaviourally-informed DHI - RecoverEsupport - in increasing adherence and improving recovery outcomes following colorectal cancer surgery. Methods A parallel-group RCT was conducted in two Australian hospitals. Adults undergoing colorectal cancer surgery were randomised (1:1) to usual care or usual care plus the RecoverEsupport DHI targeting ERAS behaviours, including early mobilisation and early oral fluid and food intake. Between-group differences in the primary (length of hospital stay (LOS)) and secondary outcomes (patient-led ERAS behaviours and quality of recovery (QoR-15)) were investigated using regression analyses within a Bayesian framework. Results On Day 1 post-surgery, there was moderate to strong evidence that the intervention was superior in increasing time out of bed [median 195 vs 60 minutes; RR=2.38, 95% CrI 1.43-3.29; Pr(Superiority)=1.000], and fluid intake [75% vs 45% consuming >/=4 cups; OR=5.67, 95% CrI 1.12-30.1; Pr(Superiority)=0.987], and moderate evidence of a small increase in time spent moving around [median 23 vs 20 minutes; RR=1.28, 95% CrI 0.9-1.86; Pr(Superiority)=0.904]. There was also moderate evidence of intervention superiority in terms of quality of recovery [mean QoR-15 difference=11.64, 95% CrI -2.97-25.63; Pr(Superiority)=0.937] exceeding the clinically meaningful difference. Conclusions Although the RecoverEsupport intervention did not reduce length of hospital stay, it increased early mobilisation, fluid intake and quality of recovery for CR surgery patients.

after.title: Preprint: Depressive Symptom Trajectories and Incident Cognitive Impairment by Outcome Ascertainment
after.authors: Liu, X. L.; Guo, Z. L.
after.abstract: Importance: Dementia prevention frameworks treat depression as a leading modifiable risk factor, but cohort estimates of the association vary widely; whether this variation reflects how cognitive outcomes are ascertained is unknown. Objective: To examine whether associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident cognitive impairment vary by outcome ascertainment rigor. Design, Setting, and Participants: This harmonized cohort study included 91,043 adults aged 50 years or older from 4 national longitudinal aging cohorts (CHARLS [China], HRS [US], ELSA [England], and SHARE [16 European countries]); baseline waves spanned 2006 to 2011, with follow-up through 2023. Exposure: Depressive symptom trajectory classes (persistent low, persistent high, incident worsening, remitting) derived using group-based trajectory modeling. Main Outcomes and Measures: Incident cognitive impairment ascertained under a 5-level hierarchy of increasing rigor, from self-report (level 1) to clinical consensus diagnosis (level 5; Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol [HCAP]). Cohort-specific Cox models were pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; meta-regression tested ascertainment rigor as a moderator of heterogeneity. Results: Under nonadjudicated outcomes, the incident-worsening trajectory was associated with incident cognitive impairment in CHARLS (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.06-1.62) and SHARE (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.87-2.13) but not HRS (HR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.95-1.16) or ELSA (HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.95-1.27); the persistent-high trajectory was not significant under any nonadjudicated outcome (HR range, 1.07-1.15). Under clinical consensus diagnosis (n = 3,196), all non-low trajectories were independently associated with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (OR range, 1.66-2.29; dementia-only persistent high: OR, 3.32; 95% CI, 1.85-5.95). Effect sizes increased stepwise with ascertainment rigor (meta-regression slope, 0.314 log HR per level; P < .001; residual I2 = 0%; R2 = 100%; exploratory). Findings were robust to lagged, weighted, and competing-risk analyses; biological aging acceleration did not differ across trajectories. Conclusions and Relevance: The detectability and magnitude of depression-related cognitive risk depend on outcome ascertainment rigor. Prevention trials and burden projections relying on self-reported outcomes may underestimate the benefit of depression treatment.

after.authors: Deb Nath, N.; Miljkovic, I.; Katz, R.; Hosner, J.; Mallugari, R. R.; Cvejkus, R. K.; Cruz, L. A.; Wheeler, V.; Thomas, C. N.; Gupta, D. K.; Kuipers, A. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Michigan State University, Department of Medicine, Grand Rapids, MI, USA
after.abstract: Background: Individuals of African genetic ancestry are at high risk for heart failure (HF), which is often preceded by cardiac structural and functional abnormalities. Nevertheless, little is known about cardiac structure and function among Afro-Caribbeans residing in Tobago. This study aimed to investigate the epidemiology of cardiac structure and function among African Caribbeans in Tobago. Methods: A total of 924 participants (41-83 years) underwent clinical evaluation and transthoracic echocardiography. Images were analyzed for left ventricular (LV) mass index (MI), left atrial volume index, diastolic dysfunction (DD), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e' ratio, E/A ratio, and other echocardiographic measures. Cardiac structure and function were evaluated by age, sex, and HF stage. Results: The mean age was 61.7 years, with 61.4% women, 47.8% obesity, and 20.2% diabetes. Average systolic blood pressure was approximately 140 mmHg, and 76.7% had hypertension. Abnormal LV geometry was present in 77.1% of participants, predominantly concentric remodeling (69.5%). The prevalence of DD was 13.4%, LVEF <50% was 1.5%, and abnormal GLS ([≤]-18%) was 5.2%. Women had significantly higher E/e' ratios and a higher prevalence of Stage A and Stage B HF, whereas men had a higher prevalence of symptomatic (Stage C) HF. Participants aged 65-83 years had significantly higher E/e' ratio, concentric remodeling, and LV hypertrophy than those aged 41-57 years. Conclusions: Women and older adults have higher LV structural abnormalities and DD than men and younger adults. These results will be helpful to inform public health priorities related to cardiovascular health in Tobago.

after.title: Preprint: Targeting memory consolidation in major depression via pharmacological slow-wave sleep promotion
after.authors: Schnider, L. K.; Quednow, B. B.; Stucky, B.; Mauron, J.; Di Floriano, J. R.; Rasch, B.; Dornbierer, D. A.; Bosch, O. G.; Seifritz, E.; Landolt, H.-P.; Bavato, F.
after.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) has been implicated in memory consolidation and brain plasticity and proposed as a therapeutic target in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, whether pharmacological promotion of SWS causally improves memory consolidation remains unknown. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a robust enhancer of SWS, represents a promising drug-repurposing candidate to target this pathway. We therefore conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 patients with MDD and 20 matched healthy controls receiving single nocturnal doses of GHB, trazodone as an active comparator, or placebo under polysomnographic monitoring (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04082806). Declarative, procedural and emotional memory were assessed before and after sleep. GHB strongly increased SWS duration and delta power, whereas trazodone produced smaller changes in sleep-stage composition. Contrary to our hypothesis, neither drug improved memory consolidation across domains. Exploratory analyses revealed weak associations between global sleep-stage measures and memory, alongside selective associations with spindle and spectral features. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing SWS alone is sufficient to improve overnight memory consolidation and suggest that more targeted modulation of sleep oscillatory dynamics may be required.

after.title: Preprint: Motherly Plus: Study Protocol of a Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating a Smartphone-Assisted Single-Session Psychotherapy Intervention for Postpartum Depression
after.authors: Zuccolo, P. F.; Melo, H.; Seda, L.; Borja, T.; Matijasevich, A. F.; Caye, A.; Miguel, E. C.; El Rafihi, R.; Fatori, D.
after.abstract: Introduction: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a public health problem, affecting approximately 17% of women worldwide. PPD is associated with significant costs to the healthcare system and impairments for the child. Although evidence shows that psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are effective in reducing PPD symptoms, access to these treatments is limited, especially in low- and middle-income countries where there is a shortage of professionals and unequal distribution of mental health services. In this context, telehealth, smartphone apps, and brief psychotherapies emerge as viable, low-cost, and potentially scalable alternatives. However, gaps remain regarding the efficacy of single-session psychotherapies for PPD, especially when combined with digital support. Objectives: The primary objective is to test the efficacy of an intervention package combining single-session psychotherapy with subsequent self-guided use of a smartphone app for the treatment of PPD. Secondary objectives are to investigate moderators, mediators, and specific intervention processes. Method: A randomized clinical trial in which 104 women aged 18-40 years, up to 12 months postpartum, with a diagnosis of PPD will be randomized to the intervention (single-session psychotherapy supported by the Motherly app) or a waitlist. Participants in the intervention arm will retain access to the app throughout the study; waitlist participants will receive the intervention after post-treatment assessment. Assessments will occur at T1 (week 1, baseline), T2 (week 2, mid-treatment), T3 (week 4, post-treatment), and T4 (week 8, follow-up). The primary outcome will be depression assessed by the QIDS-C16 at T3. Secondary outcomes include anxiety, sleep, parental stress, and self-reported depression. Data will be analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) models considering an intention-to-treat (ITT) perspective. Mediation models will be used to analyze mediators, while interaction models will be used to explore potential moderators. Regression models will be used to analyze the association between specific processes (therapeutic alliance and app engagement) and clinical outcomes. Perspectives: This study has potential public health relevance and innovation by testing an intervention package that combines single-session psychotherapy and technology, with high potential for scalability. Trial registration: clinicaltrials.gov NCT07925762 Key words: Postpartum depression; clinical trial; cognitive-behavior therapy; digital intervention; smartphone app; single session psychotherapy

after.title: Preprint: Unmet needs of Polish patients with cystic fibrosis seen through the lens of crowdfunding
after.authors: Kaminski, M.; Nowak, J. K.; Karp, Z.; Borys, A.; Walkowiak, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of the Treatment of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders, and of Clinical Dietetics, Poznan University of Medical Sciences Przybyszewskiego 49, 60-355, Po
after.abstract: Medical crowdfunding allows for funding for needs not covered by the local healthcare system. We aimed to characterize the crowdfunding campaigns for the needs of Polish individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). In our study, we analyzed data from a leading medical crowdfunding webpage in Poland, focusing on campaigns for individual medical needs initiated between 2009 and 2017. We characterized the features of individuals with CF and the declared goals for which the funds from the online campaigns were intended. Of all 2,656 campaigns, 96 (3.6%) were related to individuals with CF. Approximately two-thirds of these campaigns reached their target amount. Individuals with CF primarily raised funds to cover treatment costs, medical equipment, and entertainment. The successful collection had a significantly lower financial target than unsuccessful campaigns. If the receivers were living in a city or fundraising to gather funds for an inhaler, these were also associated with the campaign's success. However, these associations were slightly above the threshold of statistical significance. Crowdfunding campaigns can be an effective funding source for the needs of patients with CF that are not covered by the public healthcare system. Analyzing crowdfunding efforts for specific patient groups can help reveal their unmet health needs.

M.; West, T.; Verghese, P. B.; Russ, K. A.; Morris, A.; Lu, M.; Iaccarino, L.; Aldea-Stevenson, P.; Flitter, M.; Beck, R.; Hutten, S.; Chahine, L. M.; Weintraub, D.; Foroud, T.; Simuni, T.; Marek, K.; Merchant, K.; The Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative,
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Neurodegenerative Disorders; New Haven, CT, USA
after.abstract: Objectives: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Methods: Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (A{beta}) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. Results: The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants. Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 -49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD A{beta}40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; A{beta}42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Interpretation: Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.

after.title: Preprint: Social determination of health and intersectionality in child hunger: A multilevel qualitative comparative case study in Choco and Risaralda, Colombia
after.authors: Taborda Restrepo, P. A.; Borrero Ramirez, Y. E.; Mancilla Lopez, L. P.
after.abstract: Acute child malnutrition has historically been approached in public health as an individual nutritional deficit, despite its persistence in territories marked by structural inequity. This study analyzed how the general, particular, and singular domains of the social determination of health articulate with the intersectional axes of gender, ethnicity, class, and territory in the social production of child hunger in Choco and Risaralda, two Colombian departments with a high burden of acute child malnutrition. We conducted a qualitative comparative case study grounded in a socio-critical paradigm and a critical feminist epistemology, based on fieldwork carried out in 2024. In-depth interviews with 28 participants--mothers and caregivers, health workers, and decision-makers--were combined with a field diary and a documentary review. Analysis followed open coding, axial coding, and categorical integration, yielding 722 coded units and 207 analytical categories, which were organized through a convergence matrix across the three domains of social determination and the intersectional axes. In the particular domain, informal work, food restriction, and institutional fragmentation shaped ways of life marked by the feminization of care, while formally established care pathways failed to sustain nutritional recovery. In the singular domain, trajectories of accumulated violence, forced early unions, and female genital mutilation preceded and shaped motherhood under precarious conditions, together with guilt, anguish, and fear produced by the institutional moralization of maternal care. Across domains, structural conditions were subsumed into collective ways of life and embodied in singular trajectories, without cancelling situated forms of agency, resistance, and care. A multilevel integration of social determination and intersectionality allows child hunger to be understood as a historically produced process that simultaneously traverses structures, ways of life, and bodies, and that cannot be resolved through exclusively clinical or welfare-based responses. The proposed model offers a transferable analytical tool for critical public health research seeking to integrate structural, collective, and biographical evidence.

after.abstract: Importance: Accelerated protocols have emerged over the past two decades as a promising method of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) administration that allows for shorter treatment duration and faster time to response. Although recent research has suggested accelerated TMS may be noninferior to daily TMS on clinical outcome measures, no studies have directly compared the neural effects of daily and accelerated TMS within the same participant group. Objective: Compare the neural effects of daily vs accelerated TMS applied to a personalized default mode network (DMN) target on bilateral parietal DMN connectivity in a transdiagnostic sample (n=36) before and after TMS. Design: Within-subjects crossover design. Setting: Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN. Participants: 36 individuals with a range of psychiatric conditions were enrolled (e.g., psychosis, depression, anxiety). Data from 34 participants are included in analysis. Intervention: 5 daily sessions of DMN-targeted continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) with pre-/post neuroimaging. After a washout period (mean =379.26 days), these same participants returned for 5 accelerated sessions of DMN-targeted cTBS in one day with pre-/post neuroimaging. Main Outcome and Measure: To compare the neural effects of accelerated versus traditional daily TMS schedules, the primary outcome measure was change in resting-state bilateral parietal DMN connectivity between pre-TMS and post-TMS. Results: Across all participants and both treatment schedules, DMN-targeted cTBS reduced bilateral parietal DMN connectivity (t(90.16)=-2.07, p=0.0416). TMS schedule did not did not have a statistically significant effect in DMN connectivity change(t(31.27) = -0.44, p = 0.67) . Psychosis diagnosis did not affect bilateral parietal DMN connectivity change (t(28.34)=-0.53, p=0.601). However, older age was associated with greater reduction in bilateral parietal DMN connectivity across the entire sample (t(26.91)=-2.21, p=0.036). Conclusion and Relevance: This study suggests accelerated and daily TMS protocols may have comparable neural effects across psychiatric diagnoses. Understanding the effects of TMS schedule is critical for protocol design and clinical TMS application. Trial Registration: NCT07155096 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07155096), NCT06389266 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06389266)

after.title: Preprint: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
after.authors: Shahdadian, S.; Song, Y.; Vaysi, A.; Christian, R.; Bosemani, M.; Acosta, F.; Kimbrell, B.; Marks, W.; Papadelis, C.
after.abstract: Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization (P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho = -0.74 to -0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization (Rho = -0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization (Rho = -0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q^2 = 0.42, P < 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q^2 = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03-0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.

after.title: Preprint: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
after.authors: Chen, L.; Witt, L.; Calvano, A.; Bopp, M. H. A.; Nimsky, C.; Dafsari, H. S.; Timmermann, L.; Pedrosa, D. J.; Belke, M.; Loehrer, P. A.
after.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

after.authors: Ogulnick, J. V.; Shin, W.; Mathew, J.
after.abstract: Background: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common neurological disorder with established links to atherosclerotic disease and secondary causes such as ischemic stroke. Hypothesizing that internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS) could induce secondary RLS through chronic hypoperfusion or microemboli to dopaminergic subcortical structures, even without overt stroke, we investigated the association between bilateral CAS and RLS. Methods: A retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study was conducted using the TriNetX Global Health Research Network. Cases (n=58,382) had bilateral CAS/occlusion (ICD-10-CM I65.23); controls (n=58,382) had atherosclerosis without CAS. Patients were excluded for prior stroke/TIA, iron deficiency, antipsychotic use, and other secondary RLS causes. Cases and controls were 1:1 matched on age, race/ethnicity, chronic kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease, Parkinson's disease, and SSRI use. The outcome was RLS diagnosis (G25.81), assessed via conditional logistic regression. Results: RLS was diagnosed in 1,154 (1.977%) patients with bilateral CAS/occlusion versus 1,060 (1.816%) controls, yielding an absolute risk difference of 0.161% (95% CI 0.005-0.317%; p=0.0437). The adjusted odds ratio was 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186), indicating a modest but significant association. Conclusion: Severe bilateral CAS/occlusion is associated with a small but statistically significant increase in RLS risk, independently of overt cerebrovascular events and known confounders. These findings support a potential vascular contribution to RLS pathogenesis, possibly through subclinical hypoperfusion affecting basal ganglia dopaminergic pathways. Prospective studies are needed to explore causality, dose-dependency, and the impact of carotid revascularization.

after.abstract: Introduction: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is characterised by amyloid-beta (A{beta}) deposition in cerebral vessels, and frequently co-occurs with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diagnosis based on MRI-based Boston criteria is not definitive, and CAA biofluid biomarkers are needed. Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) was recently shown to be selectively enriched in CAA-affected vessels, and correlated with CAA severity. We therefore evaluated SEMA3G as a biofluid biomarker of CAA. Methods: SEMA3G profiles were examined across diagnoses in the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium dataset (GNPC) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (N=1982) and plasma (N=6917). SEMA3G was then evaluated in the Healthy Brain Ageing (HBA) memory clinic cohort (N=161) with 3T MRI, where lobar cerebral microbleed burden was used as a proxy for CAA likelihood, with participants grouped by microbleed count (0, 1-2, or [≥]3). Results: CSF and plasma SEMA3G were significantly lower in AD and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) compared to cognitively unimpaired controls in GNPC, and were associated with hypertension. Longitudinally, plasma SEMA3G declined significantly over time in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD. In the HBA cohort, plasma SEMA3G did not differ by cerebral microbleed burden on MRI, nor correlate with plasma A{beta} isoforms and white matter hyperintensities. Discussion: Although CSF and plasma SEMA3G levels were significantly lower in AD and FTD, plasma SEMA3G was not associated with CAA-associated MRI features in individuals at risk of AD. While these findings do not support plasma SEMA3G for identifying individuals with higher CAA-associated burden, its potential utility warrants further evaluation in genetically susceptible or neuropathologically confirmed CAA cohorts.

after.abstract: Background: Pathological complete response (pCR) after pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy predicts improved outcomes in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but circulating immune determinants of response remain poorly characterized. Methods: The study included 64 patients with early TNBC treated with pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Flow cytometry analyzed 125 peripheral-blood specimens collected at baseline, during treatment and before surgery. Baseline PBMCs from 22 patients underwent scRNA-seq, generating 135,271 quality-controlled cells. Analyses used nonparametric tests, effect sizes, FDR correction and sensitivity analyses. Results: Baseline scRNA-seq identified response-associated transcriptional differences. Patient-level pseudo-bulk analysis revealed enrichment of TNF-alpha/NF-kappaB signaling in cytotoxic T/NK and B cells from non-pCR patients (global q<=3.94e-7), together with MYC targets and mTORC1 signaling in cytotoxic T/NK cells (both global q=7.00e-5). T-cell analyses suggested preserved naive/memory features in pCR, while a higher proportion of CX3CR1-expressing cells within the CD4 memory/activation-like compartment was associated with pCR (q=0.0157; AUC=0.949). In B cells, pCR was associated with a nominally higher naive-like program score (P=0.029; q=0.059), supported by higher IGHM and IGHD signals, whereas XBP1 was higher in non-pCR. Flow cytometry identified treatment-associated B-cell remodeling. At pre-surgery, switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR than non-pCR patients (62.6% versus 50.0%; P=0.0086; q=0.0667; Cliff's delta=0.651; AUC=0.825) and remained nominally significant in leave-one-patient-out analyses. Early increases in unswitched-memory B-cell CD38 balance were numerically greater in non-pCR patients, whereas pre-surgery switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR patients. Conclusions: Baseline inflammatory and metabolic pathway enrichment was associated with non-pCR, whereas pCR-associated T-cell findings included a CD4 memory/activation-associated CX3CR1 signal and trends towards preserved naive/memory features. Together with time- and compartment-dependent B-cell remodeling, these findings nominate circulating transcriptional states and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics for prospective validation as candidate biomarkers of pathological response.

after.abstract: Blood DNA methylation offers a dynamic readout of inherited and acquired influences on health, creating an opportunity for risk prediction beyond polygenic scores, which are fixed at conception and have yet to demonstrate broad clinical utility. As such, we aimed to develop methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, combining technically reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and ten-year survival models, with evaluation in a single holdout that was not used for feature selection, model fitting or tuning. after.title: Preprint: Building an Auditable Reference Standard for Clinical Information Extraction from Transesophageal Echocardiography Reports
after.authors: MacKay, E. J.; Kaplan, M. S.; Yuan, M.; Chen, A. L.; Ge, Y.; Canales, L.; Yu, E.; Shad, R.; Zhang, B.; Pouch, A. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care, Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA
after.abstract: Objectives To develop an auditable, two-institution reference standard for intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) reports and evaluate whether reviewer disagreement identifies limitations in the underlying clinical information model. Materials and Methods We selected 300 reports (150 per institution) from 925 at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Washington using random sampling and enrichment for challenging documentation. Four trained abstractors applied a shared 39-variable V1 codebook. Independent paired comparisons included 297 reports; three historical reports contributed only to the final reference standard. Categorical agreement used exact agreement and unweighted Cohen's {kappa}; numeric left-ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) used exact agreement and mean absolute differences. Disagreements underwent structured expert adjudication and reason classification. Additional analyses assessed reviewer-pair, sampling-stratified, and population-weighted agreement. Results Among 11,583 formal reviewer-comparison cells, 10,293 (88.9%) were resolved by reviewer agreement and 1,290 (11.1%) required targeted expert adjudication (1,289 tasks). Codebook/schema ambiguity (40.8%) and interpretation/classification differences (25.2%) together accounted for 66.0% of targeted tasks. Adjudication was concentrated in aortic dissection, valve type, and post-intervention findings. Categorical {kappa} ranged from 0.364 to 0.960 and was inversely correlated with targeted-adjudication burden (Spearman {rho}=-0.884; 95% CI, -0.955 to -0.734). Sampling-weighted {kappa} changed by no more than 0.05 for 32 of 35 categorical variables. Discussion Structured adjudication identified recurring schema and interpretation challenges beyond individual abstraction errors, providing specific targets for information-model refinement. Conclusion As NLP and LLM-based abstraction tools move toward clinical use, the reference standards used to evaluate them require comparably rigorous development, adjudication, and independent validation.

after.authors: Ahmed, M.; Wahid, S. T.; Khondoker, G. S.; Rabbi, G.; Islam, R. M. A.; Rahman, M. M.; Rafy, A.; Islam, S.; Haque, M. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Cell, University of Dhaka, Dhaka 1000, Bangladesh
after.abstract: Objective: To test whether a smart contract that admits hospital-trained models to a shared mortality model only after peer hospitals verify their performance can exclude poisoned or substituted models, and at what cost. Design: Retrospective simulation study of a federated learning protocol. Methodology: In the Blockchain-Enabled Federated Ensemble (BFE), hospitals committed SHA-256 digests of locally trained XGBoost and random-forest models to a Solidity contract; peers posted digest-bound validation AUROCs, and the contract admitted models with a median peer AUROC of at least 0.70. Admitted models were pooled by weighted logit averaging (BFE-PW) or stacking (BFE-Stack) with federated recalibration. Code and drafts were produced with an AI coding assistant under the authors' supervision. Setting: Four hospitals simulated from one academic centre with age, renal case-mix and laboratory-availability skew; a data-scarce regime keeping 5-20% of each hospital's patients; and a natural partition by care era. Participants: 425,215 adult admissions (186,103 patients; 2.35% in-hospital mortality) in MIMIC-IV v3.1, with predictors from the first 24 hours. Interventions: BFE against centralised, local-only, FedAvg, FedProx, median and Multi-Krum FedAvg and federated logistic regression, under seven attacks on training, attestation, recalibration and model delivery. Main outcome measures: AUROC and AUPRC (joint patient-clustered bootstrap), calibration, attack effects, gas and transactions. Results: Under gross label flipping, FedAvg lost 29% of its AUPRC while the contract excluded the poisoned models in every seed (Multi-Krum FedAvg was equally protected); all substituted models were detected, and collusion blocked release. A targeted flip of female deaths passed the gate and lowered sensitivity for deaths in women from 32.8% to 27.5%; poisoned recalibration inverted BFE-PW (AUROC 0.098) unless a median-of-sites recalibration was used (0.902). With large hospitals, BFE-PW matched FedAvg in AUROC (0.902) and BFE-Stack matched FedProx (0.907 and 0.906), below local-only (0.910) and centralised XGBoost (0.915), with lower AUPRC; with 5% of the data, BFE-PW exceeded local models (0.866 against 0.844). Pooled calibration hid two-fold under-prediction at one hospital (observed-to-expected ratio 2.13), which a local intercept corrected (0.93). One aggregation used 37 transactions and 3.3 million gas, rising roughly quadratically with consortium size. Conclusions: Contract-enforced peer attestation gave auditable, automatic exclusion of grossly poisoned and substituted models at a small accuracy cost, but did not detect attacks that preserve validation discrimination. It is most useful for consortia of small hospitals that need a verifiable record of which models entered a shared tool.

after.title: Preprint: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
after.authors: Arceri, C.; Angelis, E.; Heesen, P.; Melnychuk, V.; Bendszus, M.; Bauer, S.; Feuerriegel, S.
after.abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

after.title: Preprint: REMI: A Free Tool for Truncated Proximity Searching in PubMed
after.authors: Alebeek, R. v.; Verdonschot, R. G.
after.abstract: Background: PubMed is the most comprehensive freely available database for medical and health sciences publications, making it an essential platform for literature searching in budget-constrained settings (e.g. non-academic hospitals). However, unlike subscription platforms (e.g. Ovid MEDLINE), it cannot combine truncation with proximity operators. Searchers must therefore either enumerate every word form manually, risking missed variants, or fall back on Boolean AND, which retrieves many irrelevant records. We developed REMI (Related Expression Machine Identification), a free, open-source web application which emulates truncated proximity searching in PubMed. Case Presentation: REMI was developed at Maastricht University Library. Through the NCBI E-utilities, it identifies the variants of truncated terms that occur in PubMed records. An iterative exclusion procedure, which reruns the search for each concept while excluding that concept's variants already found, surfaces progressively rarer forms. Users select relevant variants from frequency-ranked lists, and REMI combines them into native PubMed proximity clauses that can be documented, peer reviewed, and rerun without REMI. Performance of REMI was evaluated by comparison to four Ovid MEDLINE search strategies from published reviews. REMI's proximity search was able to identify all included articles found with the original Ovid MEDLINE query. Conclusions: REMI makes truncated proximity searching available in PubMed while keeping searches transparent, reliable, and reproducible, which particularly benefits searchers without access to subscription platforms. Because variant discovery is a sampling procedure, completeness is not guaranteed, and long searches require variant selection. Other libraries can use, host, or adapt the tool, however, native support in PubMed would remain the preferable solution.

after.title: Preprint: Alignment and expansion in national adaptation of the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines: a cross-national analysis
after.authors: Kohno, Y.; Estill, J.; Moja, L.; Keiser, O.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Global Studies Institute, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland
after.abstract: Background: The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) provides a common global reference for national medicines selection. National adaptation frequently involves both the adoption of WHO-recommended medicines and the addition of medicines beyond WHO EML, which have not been distinguished in comparative analyses. This study quantifies how countries adapt the WHO EML by distinguishing alignment from expansion, exploring country-level characteristics potentially associated with these dimensions. Methods: We compared national essential medicines lists (NEMLs) from 137 countries with the WHO EML. We constructed two independent measures: the Alignment Ratio, representing the proportion of WHO-recommended medicines included in each NEML, and the Expansion Ratio, representing the proportion of NEML medicines not included in the WHO EML. Countries were also classified into four adaptation modes based on combinations of alignment and expansion. Associations with country-level characteristics were examined using multivariable beta regression. Results: Countries displayed substantial heterogeneity in adaptation patterns, with representation across all four adaptation modes defined by alignment with and expansion beyond the WHO EML. Fifty countries were categorized as restrictive/constrained adoption (low alignment, low expansion), thirty-five countries as normative dependence (high alignment, low expansion), sixteen countries as autonomous divergence (low alignment, high expansion) and thirty-six countries as capacity-driven expansion (high alignment, high expansion). Higher under-five mortality was associated with lower alignment ({beta} = -0.294; 95% CI: -0.497 to -0.091) and lower expansion ({beta} = -0.481; 95% CI: -0.697 to -0.264). Higher globalization index scores and more recent NEMLs were associated with higher alignment, but not expansion. Conclusion: While some countries closely followed the WHO EML with limited additions, a substantial proportion combined high alignment with extensive expansion beyond the WHO benchmark, suggesting that national adaptation often involves supplementation rather than substitution of WHO recommendations.

after.title: Preprint: Methamphetamine use reshapes cellular and plasma immune signatures in a lineage-specific manner in people with HIV
after.authors: Sens, J. P.; Kumar, A.; Towe, S. L.; Park, S. H.; Hsu, F.-C.; Zimmerman, K. D.; Khanna, A. K.; Solingapuram Sai, K. K.; Romero-Sandoval, E. A.; Deep, G.; Meade, C. S.; Kiraly, D. D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine
after.abstract: Methamphetamine use is common among people with HIV (PWH) and is associated with worse neurocognitive and clinical outcomes, but how it reshapes HIV-associated immune dysregulation across cell types and compartments is unknown. In this cross-sectional and observational study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from controls without HIV, PWH without methamphetamine use and PWH who use methamphetamine, then scored pathway enrichment, cytokine response and transcription factor activity in each cell population. We then profiled plasma from the same three groups in a larger set of participants by targeted proteomics, with PWH who use cocaine added as a stimulant comparison. In the single-cell data, methamphetamine use acted in opposite directions across lineages. HIV-associated changes were reversed most often in monocytes and CD8+ T cells, with interferon, antigen presentation and JAK-STAT programs shifting in monocytes and IFN-{gamma}, IL-2 and MYC programs shifting in CD8+ T cells, whereas HIV-associated proliferative and TNF signaling programs persisted in CD4+ and {gamma}{delta} T cells of Meth+HIV participants. Central memory CD8+ T cells of Meth+HIV participants showed reduced type 1 effector programs. In plasma, HIV was associated with a cytotoxic lymphocyte activation signature (KLRK1, IFN-{gamma}, TNF, granzyme B and CXCL9) that was further elevated with methamphetamine use, together with higher IL-6, CXCL13 and neurofilament heavy chain. IFN-{gamma} was the most connected protein in the plasma interaction network, linking a cytotoxic module to a lymphoid chemokine module. These data define lineage- and compartment-specific immune consequences of methamphetamine use in PWH and nominate IFN-{gamma} signaling, acting through monocyte antigen presentation and CD8+ T cell effector programs, together with TNF, IL-6 and CXCL13, as candidate mediators of neuroimmune dysfunction in PWH who use methamphetamine.

Methods: We sampled nine wasp-allergic individuals before and 7 days and 6 months after initiation of VIT, and 5 non-allergic donors at one time point. Single-cell RNA sequencing of isolated venom-specific T cells was used to characterise changes to immunophenotypes and immune receptor repertoires during VIT. Results: We unveiled a broad phenotype diversity among venom-specific T cells, which were altered during VIT. Most notably, IL5Th2 cells strongly correlated with Ves v 5-specific IgE levels at baseline, whereas their increase during VIT was associated with protective humoral immune responses, determined by the Ves v 5-specific IgG4/IgE ratio. Moreover, VIT induced exhaustion markers in Tconv, whereas Tregs acquired an activated phenotype, which was associated with increased specific IgG4 levels. T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire analysis revealed a highly polyclonal repertoire and substantial clonal expansion and plasticity in Tconv. By contrast, Treg clonotypes emerged during VIT, with no evidence of Tconv-to-Treg conversion. Conclusion: VIT induces early phenotypic changes in venom-specific T cells, which are associated with a protective IgG4 response. In particular, IL5Th2 and activated Tregs may represent candidate biomarkers of both antigen-specific sensitisation and VIT response and suggest a potential role of IL-5-related pathways in allergen-specific tolerance development. Furthermore, Tconv and Tregs TCR repertoires remained separated during VIT, opposing the Tconv-to-Treg transition hypothesis.

after.abstract: Background Echocardiographic image quality influences clinical interpretation, yet its definition remains subjective and its impact on artificial intelligence (AI) systems has not been systematically evaluated. We developed EchoQuality, a deep-learning model for automated echocardiography quality assessment, and quantified the effect of image quality on AI performance across a broad range of tasks. Methods A multidisciplinary co-creation process established a definition of echocardiographic image quality, which was used to annotate 6,474 videos for EchoQuality development and internal testing, and 1,000 videos for external testing. The impact of image quality on the performance of state-of-the-art AI models was subsequently assessed for the prediction of 12 measurements, and the detection of 5 moderate dysfunctions and 6 cardiac diseases across five international cohorts totalling 762,588 videos from 25,205 echocardiography studies. In addition, a quality-aware aggregation strategy was developed to mitigate the impact of low-quality images. Results EchoQuality achieved a performance comparable to the inter-observer agreement, while the agreement with an expert in a prospective, blinded best-clip selection experiment was 90.4%. In downstream AI uses, high-quality studies resulted in the highest performance in 97 of 122 (80%) of evaluations. The median performance gaps between high- and low-quality videos were 10% [5-20%] in the prediction of quantitative measurements (R2), 14% [7-20%] in the identification of moderate dysfunctions (sensitivity), 12% [3-20%] in the detection of diseases (sensitivity), 12% [9-15%] in view identification (accuracy), and 3% [2-5%] in left-ventricular segmentation (Dice score). Performance gaps were consistent across state-of-the-art models, datasets, and tasks. Finally, a quality-aware aggregation strategy improved performance in 88% (63 of 72) of the evaluations, with a median relative improvement of 5% [1-15%]. Conclusions EchoQuality provides an automated assessment of echocardiographic image quality, a major determinant of AI performance. Incorporating quality-awareness may improve the robustness and clinical reliability of echocardiographic AI systems.

after.abstract: The prognostic significance of tumor mutational burden (TMB) in melanoma remains controversial. One potential reason for the mixed results is that total TMB treats all mutations as biologically equivalent, despite evidence that different types of mutations contribute differently to a tumor's neo-antigenic profile. In particular, UV-induced and non-UV mutations may have distinct effects on tumor behavior and outcomes, but this hypothesis has been studied primarily in advanced-stage disease. We analyzed 656 stage II/III tumors from the InterMEL study to evaluate whether UV TMB and non-UV TMB are associated with melanoma-specific mortality and clinicopathologic factors. Higher UV TMB was associated with improved outcomes, while non-UV TMB was not associated with mortality. These findings suggest that an association between total TMB and outcome may be driven disproportionately by mutations associated with UV mutagenesis. Although this has previously been reported in advanced melanomas, our work demonstrates that the prognostic relevance of UV TMB extends to stage II/III tumors typically found in the clinical context. Whether this relationship reflects differences in tumor neo-antigenicity, immune recognition, or other biological properties remains to be determined.

after.abstract: Background: - Type 2 Diabetes mellites and Metabolic syndrome are global public health problems, and their burden is rising, particularly in developing countries. Metabolic syndrome (syndrome X, insulin resistance syndrome) consists of a constellation of metabolic abnormalities that confer increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes mellitus. There are limited data on prevalence of metabolic syndrome in type II DM patients in Ethiopia and in the horn of Africa at large, and no research has been done in our institution on this topic. Objective: - To determine the prevalence of metabolic syndrome and its associated factors in patients with type 2 diabetes on follow up at Asella Referral and Teaching Hospital diabetes follow up clinic, Asella, Oromia, Ethiopia. Method: - Cross-sectional, prospective, hospital-based survey was conducted to assess the prevalence of metabolic syndrome and its associated factors in type II DM patients among those who visited diabetic follow-up clinic of Asella referral and teaching Hospital. All type II DM patients, who visited the diabetic follow-up clinic in the study period was included in the study. 285 participants were selected using systemic random sampling technique. Data was collected from patients and their chart and filled on a checklist by trained data collectors. Data was entered to epi-data cleared and analyzed by SPSS version 26.0 and Odds ratio with 95% CI and P-value of <0.05 was considered for declaring level of significance. Results: - Using the NCEP-ATP III criteria the magnitude of Metabolic syndrome was 75.1% in this study. Among the components of Metabolic syndrome high blood pressure was the commonest (70.9%) followed by low HDL Cholesterol (70.5%), high Triglyceride (46%) and high Waist circumference (12.6%) respectively. Female and Male had comparable prevalence of Metabolic syndrome and the study showed that 55.4% of participants were taking Lipid lowering medications. Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed four factors; frequency of taking Meat (AOR = 2.47; 95% CI = 1.323-4.6), Alcohol intake (AOR = 2.79; 95% CI = 1.146-6.806), total Cholesterol level (AOR = 2.72; 95% CI = 1.023-7.224) and LDL Cholesterol level (AOR = 2.31; 95% CI = (1.029-5.161) were significantly associated with Metabolic syndrome according to this study. Conclusion: - In this study the magnitude of Metabolic syndrome was found to be 75.1% and the associated factors were Alcohol intake, Frequency of taking Meat, Total and LDL Cholesterol level. Recommendation: - Counseling of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients on the need of decreasing Alcohol and Meat consumption and physicians need to improve the habit of prescribing Lipid lowering medication. Key words: Metabolic syndrome, Type II diabetes, Cardiovascular disease, Waist circumference, Alcohol intake, Cholesterol level.

after.title: Preprint: DYCAST early warning system for dengue virus risk areas, Ribeirao Preto, Brazil
after.authors: Carney, R. M.
after.abstract: Dengue is currently the fastest-spreading vector-borne disease, with an estimated 100-400 million infections per year and nearly 6 billion people at risk--more than half the world's population. However, there is no specific antiviral treatment, thus the primary method for preventing infection is through targeted control of the principal mosquito vector, Aedes aegypti. The objective of this retrospective study is to evaluate the efficacy of forecasting dengue risk using human cases and an adaptation of DYCAST: a biologically based, spatiotemporal clustering model that proved operationally successful as a West Nile virus early warning system. Results demonstrate that DYCAST provided accurate and early detection of high-risk areas for dengue in Ribeirao Preto, Brazil, including a cryptic interepidemic focus of transmission preceding a severe epidemic. Using suspected cases, DYCAST predicted 90.3% (4,237/4,690) of confirmed cases, with a mean lead time of 66.3 days prior to illness onset. High-risk cells had >10x higher relative risk of containing a confirmed case, and sensitivity and specificity were 83.8% and 72.3%. These findings suggest that DYCAST could be utilized in real time to prospectively identify areas at high risk of dengue, for rapid and precise targeting of mosquito mitigation and public education. Implementation using free, open-source software offers a scalable technological strategy for the prevention and control of dengue around the world.
